before.label: Comparative historical sociology
before.description: Compares how states, rights, class relations and collective struggles change. Moore studies agrarian routes; Skocpol combines state breakdown with class and international relations; Tilly follows contention; Mann maps intersecting power networks. Bendix, Goldstone, Somers and Block supply different questions about authority, demography, citizenship and economic institutions. Sewell’s exchange with Skocpol makes ideology an explicit debate.

strands.title: Comparing crises and their different outcomes
strands.focus: Goldstone compares England and the Fronde, then distinguishes Castile from the Spanish monarchy’s rebellious peripheries. Similar pressures need not produce identical outcomes. Perry values the comparison but questions how far its claims travel across different societies and periods.

before.relationship: Goldstone combines demographic pressures with institutions and elite relations to explain state crises
before.evidence_note: Publisher description supports a specific comparative application. It does not establish population as a sufficient cause, consensus among demographers, or the validity of every estimate.

after.relationship: Goldstone combines demographic pressures with institutions and elite relations to explain state crises
after.evidence_note: Publisher description supports a specific comparative application. It does not establish population as a sufficient cause, consensus among demographers, or the validity of every estimate. Primary preface xxi–xxvi and comparison 156–169 now support the conjunctural argument. Fiscal pressure alone does not explain the contrasting regional cases; Perry’s review questions the breadth of generalization without reducing the book to simple Malthusianism.

outcomes.finding: Goldstone’s original preface and complete France/Spain comparison distinguish demographic/institutional conjunctions, state crisis and divergent outcomes. Castile supplies a contrast to the monarchy’s rebellious peripheries. Perry’s full contemporary review appreciates the comparative contribution while questioning how readily its claims extend across societies and periods. This addresses the Goldstone option in the bounded question; Moore’s full book is not newly read.
outcomes.research_limit: Primary Goldstone 1991 OCR title/imprint, preface xxi–xxvi and complete comparison 156–169 read, with partial adjacent 170–172. No scan collation, statistical reconstruction, archival audit, full England/France chapters or Asian chapters. The preface’s own admission of weaker Asian data is retained as a methodological limit. Separate 2016 preview title/imprint/contents read, but no post-2000 additions enter the mapped argument. Perry’s complete 1992 review on 827 visually read from official publisher image; adjacent reviews excluded. Her criticisms concern comparative reach and do not constitute re-estimation of the model or a settled verdict on its historical cases. Kuran and Moore/Skocpol results were leads only, not substantive sources for this batch.
